name: Tu Youyou
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Tu graduated from Beijing Medical College in 1955 at age 24 and was assigned to the Academy of Traditional Chinese Medicine, but her landmark artemisinin discovery came in the early 1970s when she was around 41-42.
early_history_summary: Tu studied pharmacology at Beijing Medical College, graduating in 1955 at age 24. She was assigned to the newly established Academy of Traditional Chinese Medicine and spent the late 1950s and 1960s in routine research positions before being appointed head of Project 523 in 1969.
family_context_summary: Born in Ningbo in 1930; family stressed education for Tu and her four brothers. She contracted tuberculosis at 16, which motivated her to study medicine.
evidence_summary: Tu Youyou graduated at 24 and began a research career, but her Nobel-winning artemisinin work did not begin until 1969 when she was 39. No material, independently verifiable milestone occurred by age 26.

name: Mariusz Pudzianowski
milestone_by_age_26: Won Poland's Strongest Man in 1999 at age 22, then finished 4th at the 2000 World's Strongest Man and won his first WSM title in 2002 at age 25.
early_history_summary: Pudzianowski began Kyokushin karate at age 11 and strength training at 13, coached by his weightlifter father. He won the Polish Bench Press Championship at 16, then entered his first strongman competition in 1999, winning Poland's Strongest Man and debuting at the World's Strongest Man.
family_context_summary: Born in Biała Rawska, Poland; father Wojciech was a weightlifter who became a strength coach, providing early domain exposure and training guidance.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a weightlifter and strength coach who introduced Mariusz to strength training from a young age.
evidence_summary: Pudzianowski benefited from his father's weightlifting background and early introduction to strength training at 13. His exceptional physical abilities were evident early, winning a national bench press title at 16. By 22 he was Poland's Strongest Man, and by 25 he won the first of a record five World's Strongest Man titles. The combination of genetic physical talent and early domain exposure from his father was the dominant advantage.
starting_point: Born in Biała Rawska, Poland to a working-class family; father Wojciech was a weightlifter and strength coach who introduced Mariusz to strength training from childhood.
current_position: Retired from strongman and MMA competition; runs businesses in Poland including a transport company; widely regarded as one of the greatest strongmen of all time with 5 WSM titles.

trajectory.event: Won the Polish Bench Press Championship, pressing 160 kg in his competitive debut.
Won Poland's Strongest Man and entered his first international strongman competition.
Finished 4th at the World's Strongest Man contest in his WSM debut.
Won his first World's Strongest Man title, the first of a record five career wins.
Won his fifth and final World's Strongest Man title, cementing his status as the most decorated strongman in history.
Began a mixed martial arts career in the KSW league, eventually compiling a 17-7 record.

name: Olivier Panis
milestone_by_age_26: Won the French Formula Renault championship in 1989 at age 23, establishing himself as a rising single-seater talent; followed by French F3 runner-up in 1991 at age 25.
early_history_summary: Panis grew up in Lyon with a mechanic father who did hillclimbs and bought him a kart at a young age. He raced karts for six years, trained as a mechanic, and worked at a garage while karting before winning the Volant Elf scholarship at the Winfield School in 1987, launching his single-seater career.
family_context_summary: Born in Oullins, Lyon to a mechanic father Philippe who ran a garage and competed in hillclimbs; father bought him a kart and served as his mechanic for three years.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a mechanic and amateur hillclimb racer who introduced Olivier to motorsport, bought his first kart, and acted as his kart mechanic. Olivier also worked as a mechanic at his father's garage.
evidence_summary: Panis grew up immersed in motorsport through his father, a mechanic and hillclimb racer who bought him a kart and served as his mechanic. He spent six years in karting while working as a mechanic, then won the prestigious Volant Elf scholarship at Paul Ricard in 1987, which funded his entry into Formula Renault. He won the French Formula Renault title in 1989 at age 23, runner-up in French F3 in 1991, and the International F3000 championship in 1993 before reaching F1 at 27.
starting_point: Born in Oullins, Lyon, France to a mechanic father who ran a garage and competed in amateur hillclimbs; working-class family with deep motorsport involvement.
current_position: Retired from professional racing; last competed in F1 in 2004 for Toyota and in the 24 Hours of Le Mans through 2011; father of racing driver Aurélien Panis.

trajectory.event: Won the Volant Elf scholarship at the Winfield Racing School at Paul Ricard, funding his entry into Formula Renault.
Won the French Formula Renault championship, establishing himself as a rising single-seater talent.
Finished runner-up in the French Formula 3 championship.
Won the International Formula 3000 championship with DAMS, earning an F1 seat with Ligier.
Made his Formula 1 debut with Ligier, finishing 11th in the drivers' standings with a surprise 2nd at Hockenheim.
Won the Monaco Grand Prix, his only F1 victory, from 14th on the grid in a wet race.

name: Svetlana Kapanina
milestone_by_age_26: Became Absolute Champion of Russia in aerobatics in 1991 at age 22, then won silver at the European Aerobatic Championships in 1993 at age 24, her first international medal.
early_history_summary: Kapanina grew up in Shchuchinsk, Kazakhstan, doing gymnastics for six years and various sports. She graduated from pharmacy school in 1987 and started flying at age 19 in 1988 at a DOSAAF aviation club, progressing rapidly to Master of Sport by 1990 and national champion by 1991.
family_context_summary: Born in Shchuchinsk, Kazakh SSR; father was a taxi driver and ice figure skating vice-champion of Kazakhstan; mother was a worker. Family was working-class but athletically active.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an athlete (ice figure skating vice-champion) who encouraged sports; no direct aviation domain transfer documented.
evidence_summary: Kapanina's gymnastics background (six years, candidate for master of sports) gave her physical advantages for aerobatics. The Soviet DOSAAF aviation club system provided access to aircraft and training at no personal cost. Her coach Leonid Solodovnikov provided sustained individualized training that was central to her rapid progress from first flight in 1988 to national champion by 1991. Her father's athletic background contributed to her physical orientation.
starting_point: Born in Shchuchinsk, Kazakh SSR to a working-class family; father was a taxi driver and ice figure skating vice-champion, mother was a factory worker; grew up with strong sports involvement.
current_position: Most decorated female aerobatic pilot in history with 7 World Aerobatic Championship titles; awarded FAI Best Pilot of the Century; resides in Russia and remains active in aviation.

trajectory.event: Made her first solo flight at the Kurgan DOSAAF aviation club, transitioning from pharmacy to aviation.
Qualified as Master of Sport in aerobatics, marking elite-level proficiency.
Became Absolute Champion of Russia and USSR in aerobatics and joined the Russian national aerobatic team.
Won silver at the European Aerobatic Championships, her first international medal, and became Master of Sport international class.
Won her first World Aerobatic Championship title in the women's category, the first of seven career world titles.
Won the World Air Games overall championship and received the FAI Paul Tissandier Diploma.
Won her seventh and final World Aerobatic Championship women's title, the most in history.

name: Gustav Thöni
milestone_by_age_26: Won the overall Alpine Skiing World Cup in 1971 at age 19-20, the first of four overall titles; also won his first World Cup race in December 1969 at age 18.
early_history_summary: Thöni grew up in Trafoi, South Tyrol, where his family owned the Hotel Bella Vista and his father Georg operated a ski lift on the Stelvio Pass. He started skiing at age 3, trained by his father, and made his World Cup debut at 17 in December 1968, winning his first World Cup race the following season.
family_context_summary: Born in Trafoi, South Tyrol to a family that owned the Hotel Bella Vista (since 1875); father Georg operated a ski lift on the Stelvio Pass and served as Gustav's first coach.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Georg operated a ski lift on the Stelvio Pass and coached Gustav and his cousin Roland in their early skiing development. The family hotel was located directly at the ski slopes, providing daily access to skiing from age 3.
evidence_summary: Thöni's extraordinary early advantage came from growing up at his family's hotel in Trafoi, directly on the ski slopes, with a father who operated a ski lift on the Stelvio Pass and coached him from age 3. He could ski year-round on the glacier and observed national teams training. His cousin Roland Thöni was also a competitive skier, providing a training partner. This combination of geographic immersion, family domain expertise, and early access to facilities produced one of the most dominant technical skiers of the 1970s.
starting_point: Born in Trafoi, South Tyrol, Italy to a family that owned the Hotel Bella Vista (since 1875); father Georg operated a ski lift on the Stelvio Pass and coached Gustav from age 3.
current_position: Retired from competitive skiing since 1980; operates the family Hotel Bella Vista in Trafoi; served as personal coach to Alberto Tomba (1989-1996) and later as technical director for the Italian ski team.

trajectory.event: Made his World Cup debut and won his first World Cup race, a giant slalom at Val d'Isère in December 1969.
Won his first overall Alpine Skiing World Cup title, the first of three consecutive titles.
Won Olympic gold in giant slalom and silver in slalom at the Sapporo Winter Olympics.
Won two gold medals (slalom and giant slalom) at the FIS Alpine World Championships in St. Moritz.
Won his fourth overall World Cup title, cementing his status as the dominant technical skier of the era.
Won Olympic silver in slalom and gold in combined at the Innsbruck Winter Olympics.
Retired from World Cup competition in March 1980 after 11 seasons and 24 race victories.

name: Jan-Ove Waldner
milestone_by_age_26: Reached the European Championships singles final in 1982 at age 16, and became the youngest player to reach the Men's World Cup final in 1983 at age 18; won the World Singles Championship in 1989 at age 23.
early_history_summary: Waldner started playing table tennis at age 5-6 with his older brother Kjell-Åke in a basement in Stockholm. He joined Spårvägens BTK club at age 7-8 with his brother, where his parents were actively involved (father served as club chairman, mother sold coffee at events). He was Swedish champion for his age group by 9, attended a training camp in China at 14, and turned professional at 15.
family_context_summary: Born in Stockholm to a working-class family; father Åke was a printing/warehouse worker, mother Marianne was a shop assistant/machine operator. Parents were deeply involved in the local table tennis club Spårvägens BTK.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were not table tennis professionals but were deeply embedded in the local club culture; father served as club chairman, mother sold coffee at tournaments. Older brother Kjell-Åke (2 years older) was a constant competitive training partner from childhood.
evidence_summary: Waldner's early advantage was built on intense sibling competition with his older brother from age 5, immersion in the Spårvägens BTK club culture where his parents volunteered, and his extraordinary natural feel for the ball. A pivotal training camp in China at age 14 exposed him to elite-level dedication and technique. His technical creativity and ball control were considered prodigious from a young age, earning him the nickname 'Mozart of table tennis.' The Swedish national team system provided a high-quality competitive ecosystem.
starting_point: Born in Stockholm, Sweden to a working-class family; father Åke was a warehouse/printing worker, mother Marianne was a shop assistant; older brother Kjell-Åke was a constant table tennis rival from age 5.
current_position: Retired from professional table tennis; widely regarded as the greatest table tennis player of all time; lives in Stockholm; remains a cultural icon in China where he is known as 'Lao Wa.'

trajectory.event: Reached the European Championships singles final, losing to teammate Mikael Appelgren, announcing his talent on the international stage.
Became the youngest player to reach the Men's World Cup final and won his first Swedish national title.
Won his first World Singles Championship title at Dortmund and achieved world number 1 ranking.
Won the Men's World Cup in Chiba City, completing a career sweep of major titles.
Won Olympic gold in singles at the Barcelona Olympics, becoming one of two players to win all three major titles.
Won his second World Singles Championship title at Manchester without dropping a single set.
Won Olympic silver in singles at Sydney, reaching the final at age 35.

name: Pepe
milestone_by_age_26: Signed for FC Porto in May 2004 at age 21 and had a breakthrough 2005-06 season at age 22-23, winning the Primeira Liga and establishing himself as one of Portugal's top defenders before moving to Real Madrid in 2007.
early_history_summary: Pepe grew up in Maceió, Brazil in humble circumstances, playing for local club Corinthians Alagoano. At 18 he moved to Portugal to join Marítimo, spending his first season with the B-team before breaking into the first team. His performances earned a transfer to Porto in 2004, where he became a starter and won two league titles.
family_context_summary: Born in Maceió, Alagoas, Brazil to a humble family; arrived in Portugal with approximately 5 euros in his pocket. Father named him after scientists Kepler and Laveran.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; no evidence of family football connections.
evidence_summary: Pepe's path from poverty in Maceió to European football was driven by physical talent and determination rather than inherited advantages. He arrived in Portugal with almost no money and worked his way up from Marítimo's B-team to the first team. His physical defensive style caught Porto's attention, leading to a transfer at 21 and a breakthrough season under coach Co Adriaanse at 22-23. The move to Portugal's football ecosystem was a key structural advantage, but the primary driver was his own physical ability and grit.
starting_point: Born in Maceió, Alagoas, Brazil to a humble family; grew up playing football at local club Corinthians Alagoano before moving to Portugal at age 18 with minimal financial resources.
current_position: Retired from professional football in August 2024 at age 41; last played for FC Porto; won 3 UEFA Champions League titles with Real Madrid and Euro 2016 with Portugal; widely regarded as one of the greatest defenders of his generation.

trajectory.event: Moved from Brazil to Portugal to sign with Marítimo, starting with the B-team before breaking into the first squad.
Signed for FC Porto in May 2004, joining one of Europe's top clubs shortly before they won the Champions League.
Had a breakthrough season under coach Co Adriaanse, establishing as a starter and winning the Primeira Liga title with Porto.
Transferred to Real Madrid for a reported 30 million euros, becoming one of the most expensive defenders at the time.
Won the UEFA Champions League with Real Madrid, the first of three UCL titles (2014, 2016, 2017).
Won Euro 2016 with Portugal, starting in the final despite injury concerns.
Retired from professional football after a final stint at FC Porto, having won 141 caps for Portugal.

name: Christl Haas
milestone_by_age_26: Won the downhill gold medal at the 1962 FIS Alpine World Championships in Chamonix at age 18-19, then won Olympic gold in the downhill at the 1964 Innsbruck Olympics at age 20.
early_history_summary: Haas grew up in Kitzbühel near the famed Hahnenkamm course, one of the world's most iconic alpine skiing venues. She became the 1960 Austrian Junior Champion at age 16-17 and won an Arlberg-Kandahar race that same year, confirming her as a future champion before her World Championship breakthrough in 1962.
family_context_summary: Grew up in Kitzbühel, Tyrol, one of the world's most famous alpine skiing towns, near the Hahnenkamm course. Specific family details not documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; however, growing up in Kitzbühel provided immersion in alpine skiing culture.
evidence_summary: Haas's primary advantage was growing up in Kitzbühel, one of the world's premier alpine skiing towns, providing daily access to world-class courses and a deep skiing culture. She became Austrian Junior Champion at 16 and won a major Arlberg-Kandahar race the same year. The Austrian ski team system provided elite coaching and competition. By 18-19 she was World Champion in downhill, and by 20 she was Olympic champion.
starting_point: Born in Kitzbühel, Tyrol, Austria in 1943; grew up near the famed Hahnenkamm alpine skiing course in one of the world's most iconic ski towns.
current_position: Died on 8 July 2001 at age 57 in Manavgat, Turkey; final achievement was Olympic bronze in downhill at the 1968 Grenoble Olympics before retiring after the 1967-68 season.

trajectory.event: Became Austrian Junior Champion in alpine skiing and won an Arlberg-Kandahar race, marking her as a future champion.
Won the downhill gold medal at the FIS Alpine World Championships in Chamonix, France.
Won Olympic gold in the downhill at the Innsbruck Winter Olympics in front of her home nation's fans.
Won Olympic bronze in the downhill at the Grenoble Winter Olympics, her final major medal.
Retired from competitive skiing after the 1967-68 season, having won four World Cup downhill podiums.
Died on 8 July 2001 in Manavgat, Turkey.

name: Satoru Nakajima
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Suzuka Circuit series as a rookie in 1973 at age 20, became Japanese touring car champion in 1974 at age 21, and won the Formula Japan title in 1977 at age 24, establishing dominance in Japanese motorsport.
early_history_summary: Nakajima was born to a farming family outside Okazaki, Japan. He began driving cars in the family garden as a teenager with tips from his older brother, started karting at 16, and entered the Suzuka Circuit series in 1973, winning it as a rookie. He progressed through Japanese Formula Two, winning five championships between 1981 and 1986.
family_context_summary: Born to a farming family living just outside Okazaki, Aichi, Japan; no motorsport background in the family. He began driving cars secretly in the family garden as a teenager with his older brother's guidance.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family motorsport connections documented; older brother provided informal early driving tips.
evidence_summary: Nakajima's path to motorsport was largely self-created, growing up on a farm with no racing background. He taught himself to drive in the family garden and started karting at 16. The Suzuka Circuit, located near his home in Aichi, provided access to competitive racing. His rookie win in the Suzuka series at 20 launched a career that saw him dominate Japanese Formula Two with five titles, aided by a crucial partnership with Honda that eventually brought him to Formula 1 at 34 as the first full-time Japanese F1 driver.
starting_point: Born to a farming family just outside Okazaki, Aichi, Japan; no motorsport background; began driving cars secretly in the family garden as a teenager with his older brother's tips.
current_position: Retired from racing; runs Nakajima Racing, competing in Super Formula and Super GT; founded the Suzuka Racing School (SRS) to develop Japanese driving talent; sons Kazuki and Daisuke both became racing drivers.

trajectory.event: Won the Suzuka Circuit series as a rookie, launching his competitive racing career.
Became Japanese touring car champion driving a rotary-engined Mazda.
Won the Formula Japan title in a Nova-Honda, beginning his long association with Honda.
Won his first Japanese Formula Two championship, the first of five titles in six years.
Became the first full-time Japanese Formula 1 driver, debuting with Lotus-Honda alongside Ayrton Senna and scoring points in his second race.
Retired from Formula 1 after 80 Grand Prix starts and founded Nakajima Racing to develop Japanese motorsport talent.

name: Masashi Kishimoto
milestone_by_age_26: Naruto began serialization in Weekly Shōnen Jump in 1999 at age 24-25, becoming a massive hit that eventually sold over 250 million copies worldwide; earlier, his debut work Karakuri earned the Hop Step Award honorable mention in February 1996 at age 21.
early_history_summary: Kishimoto grew up in Okayama Prefecture as the older identical twin of Seishi Kishimoto (also a manga artist). He was obsessed with drawing from childhood, influenced by Akira Toriyama's Dragon Ball. He couldn't afford Weekly Shōnen Jump as a kid and read it at a friend's house. He attended Kyushu Sangyo University and submitted Karakuri to Shueisha in 1995, winning the Hop Step Award and launching his professional career.
family_context_summary: Born in Nagi, Okayama Prefecture as the older identical twin of Seishi Kishimoto, who also became a successful manga artist (666 Satan). Family was not affluent; Kishimoto could not afford to buy Weekly Shōnen Jump and read it at a friend's house. Grandfather told stories about war and Hiroshima.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family manga industry connections documented; twin brother Seishi pursued the same career path, suggesting shared early influences and mutual competition rather than inherited domain advantage.
evidence_summary: Kishimoto's path was driven by obsessive self-directed practice in manga creation from childhood, influenced by Akira Toriyama's Dragon Ball. His twin brother Seishi provided constant creative competition. The Hop Step Award win in 1996 earned him an editor at Shueisha, Kosuke Yahagi, who guided his early career. The structural wave of manga's global expansion in the late 1990s-2000s amplified Naruto's success. His family was not affluent, and he could not even afford the magazine he aspired to be published in.
starting_point: Born in Nagi, Okayama Prefecture, Japan as the older identical twin of Seishi Kishimoto; family was not affluent and could not afford Weekly Shōnen Jump; grandfather from Hiroshima told war stories that influenced his storytelling.
current_position: Manga artist; Naruto has sold over 250 million copies worldwide; took over as writer of Boruto: Naruto Next Generations in November 2020; created Samurai 8 (2019-2020) which was canceled; lives and works in Tokyo.

trajectory.event: Received honorable mention in Shueisha's Hop Step Award for his one-shot Karakuri, earning his first editor and launching his professional career.
Published a Naruto one-shot in Akamaru Jump Summer, the first appearance of the character that would define his career.
Naruto began serialization in Weekly Shōnen Jump, quickly becoming a hit that would run for 15 years.
Naruto anime adaptation began airing, expanding the franchise's global reach; manga sales in Japan topped 40 million copies.
Naruto manga serialization ended after 15 years, with over 250 million copies sold worldwide in 46 countries.
Launched Samurai 8: The Tale of Hachimaru in Weekly Shōnen Jump, but it was canceled in March 2020 after poor reception.
Took over as writer of Boruto: Naruto Next Generations manga, replacing Ukyō Kodachi.

name: Korado Korlević
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Korlević earned his B.Sc. in 1981 at age 22-23 and was teaching and doing amateur astronomy, but his prolific asteroid discoveries (1162 numbered minor planets) did not begin until 1996-2001 when he was in his late 30s.
early_history_summary: Korlević became active in astronomy during his college years in Pula, joining a local amateur astronomical society. After earning his B.Sc. from the pedagogical faculty of Rijeka in 1981, he spent years making telescopes and teaching at the Amateur Astronomical Society of Višnjan before co-founding the Yugoslav School of Astronomy in the late 1980s.
evidence_summary: Korlević was a teacher and amateur astronomer through his 20s with no major discoveries until his late 30s. His 1162 asteroid discoveries at Višnjan Observatory occurred during 1996-2001, well after age 26. No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Ninoslav Marina
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Marina obtained his PhD at EPFL in 2004 at age 29-30, and his notable roles (Rector 2012-2021, Director of R&D at Sowoon Technologies 2005-2007) all came after age 26.
early_history_summary: Marina was born in Skopje in 1974. Details of his early career before his PhD at EPFL (completed 2004) are not well documented in reviewed sources. His professional achievements including R&D directorship and university rectorship all occurred after age 30.
evidence_summary: Marina's documented career milestones all occurred after age 26: PhD at EPFL in 2004 (age 29-30), R&D director at Sowoon Technologies (2005-2007), visiting scholar at Hawaii (2007-2008), postdoc at Princeton (2009-2012), and Rector of UIST (2012-2021). No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 was found.
